text: Blockrotate| Senior Systems / Rust Engineer | Remote (US/EU timezones preferred) | Full-time | $130k - $170k + Equity Blockrotate ( builds low-latency copy-trading and execution infrastructure for Polymarket and prediction markets. Copy trading on prediction markets has strange market microstructure. Unlike deep perp DEXes (Binance, Hyperliquid), Polymarket orderbooks are bounded, often thin, and subject to severe adverse selection. When a high-volume leader buys, the book moves immediately. If followers lag by a few hundred milliseconds, or if a platform taxes every order with a 50bps fee, follower alpha drops to zero. Most existing tools in this space either hit users with high per-trade taker fees or ask them to export and paste their master private key into a database. We took a different approach: isolated per-bot deposit wallets (non-custodial via EIP-1967/1271 proxies) and co-located autonomous Rust workers running delta-sync loops directly against the Polymarket CLOB. Stack: - Backend: Rust, Tokio, Axum, Protobuf over WebSockets, SQLite (WAL mode) - Trading Engine: Custom Polymarket CLOB & Data API clients, EIP-712 signing, dynamic slippage ladders, momentum filters, circuit breakers - Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS What you’d actually work on: - Squeezing latency out of the execution hot path (delta position calculation, order placement, nonce handling, fill verification). - Building better execution protection: momentum filters to dodge toxic order flow, fill stabilization windows, and handling thin book liquidity without moving the market against yourself. - Scaling worker orchestration: our C2 server talks Protobuf to distributed bot workers with monotonic sequence IDs and autonomous reconnect failover. As bot volume scales, we need to keep state reconciliation bulletproof. - Investigating and exploiting prediction market quirks (rebate structures, orderbook snapshotting, MEV/relayer bottlenecks). author: possibilistic
text: I'm modeling ourselves after Valve, which strongly emphasizes on-site. Valve gives its folks tons of latitude and freedom in exchange for working together in a tightly-knit culture. I'm not a stickler for showing up to work on time, and I'm a late riser / night owl myself. But the energy of being in a room together physically is extremely hard to beat. I'm not doing this to micro-manage. I don't have time for that. I'm doing this to be a better version of myself. I get energy from working close to others, and I voraciously learn from my peers. I want people teaching me and helping me be better every single day. That might be selfish, but I thrive in that environment. What we're doing is weird and experimental and there's a metric ton of discovery in literally every path we take. A culture built around documenting and reading notes isn't going to be fast enough. I'm more hands on than someone who can write 6-pagers and read everyone else's - like Shia LaBeouf's "just do it" energy. I understand that this isn't a great fit for everyone, and I'm sorry. I'm not allergic to remote once we're bigger, but we have an enormous mandate, and I want us to tackle it like an RPG final boss in the trenches together. We have a lot to build and prove and learn. Doing it together in person reduces the network hop effects and leads to more serendipity and exchange. In a years' time, I want us to have built open source alternatives to large portions of the most used software. I want us to create a considerable shake up. I want us to have built new infrastructure to make the web more distributed and more P2P. I think we stand a better chance if we're in a room together, hacking and engineering together. That's what my gut tells me. I make films too, and that's frankly something that could never be fully remote.

text: SKIES (Visual Choices AAC) | iOS Developer, embedded at the UCLA Kasari Lab | Los Angeles | ONSITE | Full-time, 6 months | $65k ($130k annualized) 3% of children are autistic. 30% of them at age 9 remain minimally verbal: a handful of single words, never put together into a sentence. If that evokes something in you beyond the number, read on. The Kasari Lab at UCLA, one of the top autism research groups in the world, has developed a play-based intervention that helps minimally verbal autistic children. Over 24 weeks, many make real gains in communication and social connection. But it combines assistive tech setup with play improvisation, which makes it challenging to deliver, and it is not standard practice. You would build Visual Play, an app that takes pieces of this intervention (and others) and makes them easier for regular clinicians to do while playing with a child. Visual Play is funded by an NIH SBIR award to SKIES, a small Pasadena company started by Caltech alums. We make Visual Choices, one of the most-used communication apps for early communicators. This is a six-month Phase I; if the prototype works, Phase II follows, and so does the product. An ideal candidate: - is comfortable being close to, and taking feedback from, researchers and clinicians - has shipped real native iOS apps - uses AI as a force multiplier, but understands the code it produces and is not dependent on it - builds large and complex, yet maintainable, systems - is resourceful, motivated, and tenacious - is a calm, respectful presence in a research lab In person at UCLA, five days a week. author: echelon
text: To clarify from reporter mischaracterizations, this comment wasn't "gloating". This comment is a warning to my fellow software engineers that are anti-AI holdouts to look up from their place of comfort and notice what is happening in the broader world around them. Everything is changing and we can't stand still in place. If we refuse to adapt our tools and knowledge, we become worthless in whatever this new economy is going to become. This is exciting, frightening, and amazing all at once. The first 15 years of my career were not the "jet pack" future that the science fiction movies of my childhood promised me. It was cellphone incrementalism and platform lock-in. But it now feels like we're being ushered into that bold new future I dreamed of. That we might not even be able to imagine what will happen next because it could be so fantastical. I am excited, but I remain cautious. I feel like we've now become much like those who were born to witness the birth of flight and lived to see humankind land on the moon. This is our moon landing. What a time to be alive.

author: dbingham
text: > Fascism is to cancel others with opinions different to yours. No. That is not what fascism is and using the word like that saps it of all meaning. This is what Fascism is: [1] > Fascism (/ˈfæʃɪzəm/ FASH-iz-əm) is a far-right, authoritarian, and ultranationalist political ideology and movement that rose to prominence in early-20th-century Europe.[1][2][3] Fascism is characterized by support for a dictatorial leader, centralized autocracy, militarism, forcible suppression of opposition, belief in a natural social hierarchy, subordination of individual interests for the perceived interest of the nation or race, and strong regimentation of society and the economy As others have said, one can reasonable debate whether Yarvin should be identified as a fascist or "merely" an authoritarian monarchist. But either way he advocates for the replacement of democracy with an oppressive authoritarian system, is in a position of some influence and power, and is an enemy of anyone who values a free and open society. If you're not familiar with the Paradox of Tolerance, you should look it up. [2] > The paradox of tolerance is a philosophical concept suggesting that if a society extends tolerance to those who are intolerant, it risks enabling the eventual dominance of intolerance, thereby undermining the very principle of tolerance. There is a valid argument to be made that if we want a free, open, and tolerant society we can not tolerate those who publicly argue against that. We don't have to throw them in prison, but they should be "de-platformed" -- boycotted in all public spaces. Their authoritarian ideas discredited and ignored. That's what the parent comment is referring to. And that belief -- that certain ideas that threaten a free, open, and tolerant society should be discredited, de-platformed, and boycotted -- is in no way similar to fascism. [1] [2]

text: Prior Labs | Berlin, Freiburg, NYC | ONSITE | Full-time | Technical PM, ML Infra, Research Scientist/Engineer, Backend, Full Stack We build foundation models for tabular data. Deep learning transformed text and images but mostly skipped tables, which are still the data behind most clinical trials, financial models and scientific experiments. The reason is structural: no natural sequence, no spatial structure, no shared vocabulary across datasets, so the architectures and scaling laws behind LLMs don't transfer. Our approach: pre-train a transformer on millions of synthetic datasets sampled from causal-structure priors. The whole dataset goes in as context, predictions come out in one forward pass. No per-dataset training, no hyperparameter tuning, seconds instead of hours.
